description: LOSTRA is a team of three passionate explorers turning forgotten space artifacts into immersive, interactive stories. We blend space science, creativity, and technology to bring NASA’s forgotten missions back to life. We welcome creative minds in coding, design, astronomy, and storytelling.
summary:
LOSTRA (Voices of the Forgotten) is an interactive, bilingual space-learning platform that brings the stories of human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars to life. Inspired by NASA's challenge, LOSTRA transforms mission records and scientific information into an engaging educational experience for students and space enthusiasts.

Users can explore two planetary worlds through interactive 3D environments, discover historical spacecraft and surface equipment through mission locations, and learn about their journeys, purposes, discoveries, and current status. An AI-powered storytelling and question-answering system uses NASA-grounded information to deliver accessible stories and answers in Arabic and English, with supporting sources.

LOSTRA also introduces gamification through interactive mini-games, quizzes, achievements, and progress-based learning. By combining space exploration, artificial intelligence, scientific research, storytelling, and educational gaming, LOSTRA makes space history more accessible while preserving the stories of forgotten exploration hardware.
details:
LOSTRA is an interactive educational space-exploration experience designed primarily for learners aged 9–16. It transforms the history of human-made equipment left on the Moon and Mars into an engaging journey of discovery, combining scientific research, interactive exploration, AI-powered storytelling, and gamified learning.

DATA AND SCIENTIFIC FOUNDATION
LOSTRA's research catalog contains 36 main hardware records (25 lunar and 11 Martian), covering equipment from missions such as Apollo, Surveyor, Viking, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, and Ingenuity. It also includes 88 associated instruments, mission metadata, historical timelines, location information, and NASA source references. NASA imagery is linked to the relevant records, with source provenance and uncertainty preserved.

AI AND STORYTELLING
The AI system uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Rather than relying only on general model knowledge, it retrieves relevant evidence associated with the selected machine and uses Google Gemini to generate accessible, first-person explanations and answers in Arabic or English. Responses can include supporting NASA references and suggested follow-up questions. Machine-specific retrieval helps prevent information from unrelated missions from being mixed together.

TECHNOLOGY
The backend is implemented in Python using FastAPI, ChromaDB for vector storage, ONNX MiniLM embeddings for semantic retrieval, and Google's Gemini API for natural-language generation. The web experience uses a modern JavaScript stack based on Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, with Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei for 3D visualization.

INTERACTIVE LEARNING
The experience is designed around exploring the Moon and Mars, discovering historical machines, following their stories, and learning through interactive activities. Its gamification concept includes Rover Route, Signal Rescue, Mission Memory, Artifact Hunt, and Build a Lander, supported by quizzes, experience points, and achievements.

CREATIVITY AND IMPACT
LOSTRA's distinctive approach is to let learners discover the stories of forgotten exploration hardware from a more personal perspective. It transforms technical mission information into approachable educational storytelling while encouraging curiosity about engineering, robotics, astronomy, planetary science, and the history of space exploration.

DATA RESPONSIBILITY
NASA remains the source of scientific mission information and archival references. AI-generated explanations are not presented as original NASA transcripts, and uncertain locations or incomplete evidence are not represented as verified facts. The project distinguishes historical NASA media from conceptual visual material.
